replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3031 by Reviewer 8aV2

content.title: Official response to reviewer 8aV2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time and comments. We will incorporate the feedback to make the paper better.

> Though showing superior performance than SwAV in the early epochs, CARP seems to have a lower performance upper bound than SwAV. The method should be evaluated when being fully trained. The current experiments cannot prove that CARP is better than existing works.

**Response:** In Tables 1 and 2, we present different evaluation metrics for CARP pre-trained for a different number of epochs: 200, 400, and 800. So, CARP is being evaluated fully trained. Is that what the reviewer mean?

Also, note that when only using two views, CARP achieves results superior to those of SwAV and only stays behind for an instance of SwAV where multiple views are used. We did not experiment with adding multiple views to CARP because of time and resource limitations, but empirical results show that adding more views tends to increase the performance of self-supervised methods in general.

> A recent representation learning method DINO is also based on clustering or pseudo classification, which is also an online method and shows much better performance. So the significance of this work seems not that strong.

**Response:** Regarding DINO, we opted not to add results from self-supervised methods based on transformers mainly because our method is only evaluated on CNNs.  This way, we maintain the fairness of the evaluation among the methods.  Also, please note that DINO and CARP methodologies differ significantly regarding how to avoid trivial solutions. These are just different methods to accomplish the same goal. 

> The entropy penalty to avoid cluster collapse is also not novel. It has been adopted in DINO and many existing deep clustering methods.

**Response:** We agree with the reviewer that the entropy regularizer is not novel. In fact, we acknowledge this in Section 3 of the paper. However, we propose to use this regularizer in conjunction with the random partitioning strategy, which itself is novel in the context of self-supervised learning. Moreover, we show that when combining the two, we do not need to further regularize the entropy term using a scalar. Also, note that DINO does not use, in its main loss formulation, the entropy term used in our work. Instead, they combine sharpening and mean subtraction to avoid collapsed solutions as we mentioned in the last paragraph of Section 4. 

> The motivation of the random partition strategy is not clear enough. The authors claim “the benefits of using the random partition strategy is that we no longer require the hyperparameter λe to avoid trivial solutions”, but the entropy term is still adopted in the loss.

**Response:** We are sorry if the motivation and explanation of the random partition strategy are not clear enough. The motivation is to address some limitations self-supervised clustering methods usually have in avoiding collapsed solutions. The random partition strategy is the proposed antidote for this problem. It regularizes the model by providing smaller pseudo-classification tasks. Using random partitions, not only do you avoid trivial solutions, but you also get a boost in performance. Moreover, the benefits of the method can be seen in Tables 1 and 2, mainly when compared to CARL, which does not use such a strategy. Also, in the Abblations (Section 6.3), we show that training collapses without the random partition strategy. Moreover, in Section 4, when we say that we no longer require the hyperparameter $\lambda$ to avoid trivial solutions, we mean that we do not need to tune this hyperparameter because collapse is avoided by the random partitions. We will rewrite this point to make it clearer.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3031 by Reviewer VNZj

content.title: Official response to reviewer VNZj
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time and comments. We will incorporate the feedback to make the paper better.

> As for the reviews of related works based on self-supervised learning for representation learning, only self-supervised embedding prediction methods and self-supervised clustering method are reviewed, which is not complete, such as Masked Image Modeling based models for representation learning in a self-supervised style.

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for the suggestion about the literature. We will re-write the related work to add such suggested methods.

> The paper is a little confusing in explaining the model. E.g., The authors extend Silva & Ram´ ırez Rivera’s (2021) work, and are there 4 branches for student and teacher modules in total? Why only the pairs (s^1,t^2) and (s^2,t^1) are considered? How about the pairs (s^1,t^1) and (s^2,t^2) ?

**Response:** The learning framework comprises two encoders, a student and a teacher. From a pair of views, we forward each view through the encoders. This will output 4 representations. From view 1, we obtain the representations from the student and teacher, $s^1$ and $t^1$. From view 2, we obtain representations from student and teacher, $s^2$ and $t^2$. The representations are forwarded through project and assigner heads to produce probability distributions over the random partitions. You can view the partitions as subsets of the prototypes. Then, we enforce consistency between the views' assignments. That is, we want views to be assigned to the same prototypes across all partitions. 

The teacher branch is new if compared to CARL, but it is a common component in other self-supervised methods.

The reason why the pairs $(s^1, t^1)$, and $(s^2, t^2)$ are not considered is that they don’t add any extra performance improvement since they come from the same view. This is a standard practice in self-supervised learning, and we follow previous work in this regard.

> Meanwhile, the authors describe less about related models used in this paper.
>
>  Is a pair of parentheses needed in Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 after the sum operation？

**Response:** In both: the Introduction and Related Work sections, we provide a simple taxonomy to provide insights about how related models work and where our proposed algorithm fits w.r.t. them. As for the parentheses in the equations, we believe they were not needed, but we will add them for completeness.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors argue that the previous consistent assignment strategy does not scale well to enormous datasets containing a large number of classes. To solve this problem, the authors propose to use random partitions to help to regularize the model for the large dataset. Specifically, a differentiable assigner module is proposed to generate soft pseudo-labels by comparing the representations of image views to prototypes within random partition subsets. Experiments on extensive benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ Interesting and important research problem. This paper focuses on how to improve the consistent assignment strategy for the current SSL framework in the situation of large training data. This topic will attract the interest of the ICLR community.

+ The overall contribution is clear to understand. Although some details in the introduction and method parts are not very clear, the reading is comfortable and smooth. 

+ Extensive experiments focusing on large-scale datasets bring broader impacts.


Weaknesses (questions):

- The introduction is not well-aligned with the novelty. The key contribution of this paper is to remedy the consistent assignment for the enormous dataset, which is small and accurate. However, the introduction part on page 1 is all about the related work of the SSL methods, which is not highly related to the motivation and may be integrated into the related work. The authors are encouraged to spend more words explaining why CARL fails in enormous datasets. This part is still not clear yet.

- In the introduction, the authors claim that "we show that such a strategy does not scale well to enormous datasets containing millions of classes." However, 
1) Where does the author show the inferiority of CARL? It would be better to show a diagram or chart to support the claim.
2) After reading the experiment part, it seemed that the authors do not perform experiments on datasets with millions of classes.

- The contribution summarization of the introduction makes the readers confused. "A differentiable assigner" is not mentioned before in the introduction. It's hard for the readers to figure out the relationship between the differentiable assigner and the proposed CARP. What will the CARP be if there is no assigner module?

- It seemed that the most relevant work is the CARL, however, the authors did even not include it in the related work. 

- Section 3 (CONSISTENT ASSIGNMENT OF VIEWS) seems to be similar to the CARL. Is the BYOL-like slow-fast stream the key difference? If it is, then what is the role of such slow-fast stream? Since it seemed that the random partition is the key part to resolve the dimensionality problem.

- The authors are highly encouraged to add some diagrams to help to explain the random partition in section 4. The consistency assignment with random partitions is hard to understand for readers.

- As the authors claimed, the number of partition blocks can greatly affect the results. Are there any methods to quickly select the best number? Or are there any solutions to automatically decide the number?

- Compared to related works (Table 1), the proposed one shows to be marginal, and not always the top-performing one regarding the Top-1 or mAP metrics.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is poor as so many questions were raised in the above session.
Novelty is limited, since the two-branch idea is similar to BYOL, and its method is more like a CARL+a regularization.
Not sure about its reproducibility, as no complete testing code is offered in supplementary.
content.summary_of_the_review: A lot of concerns about the clarity. The authors need to justify the difference between this work and BYOL and CARL. The results are not outstanding.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3031 by Reviewer siPk

content.title: Official response to reviewer SiPk 1/2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time and comments. We will incorporate the feedback to make the paper better.

> The introduction is not well-aligned with the novelty. The key contribution of this paper is to remedy the consistent assignment for the enormous dataset, which is small and accurate. However, the introduction part on page 1 is all about the related work of the SSL methods, which is not highly related to the motivation and may be integrated into the related work. The authors are encouraged to spend more words explaining why CARL fails in enormous datasets. This part is still not clear yet.

**Response**: We agree that the key contribution of the paper is to devise a method that can be trained on large datasets without collapsing. 
We address this point beginning from the second paragraph of the Introduction section. Moreover, regarding why CARL fails, you can find an insightful explanation in the Introduction Section starting from the 5th paragraph. Also, starting from the 7th paragraph of Section 3, we detail at length why CARL fails when learning representations from complex datasets. We will expand this explanation to make it clearer for the reader in the revised manuscript.

> In the introduction, the authors claim that "we show that such a strategy does not scale well to enormous datasets containing millions of classes." However, where does the author show the inferiority of CARL? It would be better to show a diagram or chart to support the claim.

**Response**: The superiority of CARP over CARL is demonstrated in Table 1 and in the Ablations (Section 6.3). Table 1 shows that CARP achieves better results across different metrics and tasks. In the Ablations (Section 6.3), we show that training collapses without the random partition strategy (last column of Table 5). We highlight that the cell in the last row and last column of Table 5 is equivalent to the setup in CARL (we acknowledge that having a better naming convention in the table will make it easier for the reader to follow). We will improve this section to make this comparison clearer to the reader. 

> After reading the experiment part, it seemed that the authors do not perform experiments on datasets with millions of classes.

**Response**: We would love to run CARP on more complex datasets, but unfortunately, resources are a limitation. Despite not including experiments with millions of classes, our experiments are comparable against other recently published methods [1, 2, 3].

[1] Lee, Kyungmin. "Prototypical Contrastive Predictive Coding."ICLR 2021.

[2] Bardes, Adrien, Jean Ponce, and Yann LeCun. "VICRegL: Self-Supervised Learning of Local Visual Features." Neurips, 2022.

[3] Assran, Mahmoud, et al. "Masked siamese networks for label-efficient learning."ECCV, 2022.

> The contribution summarization of the introduction makes the readers confused. "A differentiable assigner" is not mentioned before in the introduction. It's hard for the readers to figure out the relationship between the differentiable assigner and the proposed CARP. What will the CARP be if there is no assigner module?

**Response**: We are sorry that the description of "A differentiable assigner" was unclear in the Introduction. In the paper, the assigner is represented as a function $q(\cdot)$ that linearly combines the views' embeddings with the learnable prototypes. The goal is to discretize the embedding space and devise pseudo-classification problems to assign views to the same prototypes over the random partitions. In the paper, we depicted and explained it in Figure 1, in the second paragraph of Section 3, and in Appendix B1. Despite these references, we will review the Introduction to make it clear and easy for the reader to follow. 

Our assigner makes CARP different from other methods, such as SwAV, which needs a non-differentiable algorithm to solve the cluster assignment problem. Instead, we do it online using gradient descent. 

> It seemed that the most relevant work is the CARL, however, the authors did even not include it in the related work.

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. While introducing the problem and motivation (Section 1), we mentioned CARL, and we refer to its performance in Table 1. However, we missed that there may be needed more descriptions to convey the method. In the revised manuscript, we will also discuss CARL in the related work for the sake of completeness.

replying_to: Replying to Official response to reviewer SiPk 1/2

content.title: Official response to reviewer siPk 2/2
content.comment:
> Section 3 (CONSISTENT ASSIGNMENT OF VIEWS) seems to be similar to the CARL. Is the BYOL-like slow-fast stream the key difference? If it is, then what is the role of such slow-fast stream? Since it seemed that the random partition is the key part to resolve the dimensionality problem.

**Response**: The reviewer is right about the random partition being key to solving the dimensionality problem and avoiding trivial solutions. Indeed, that is the key difference from CARL. In the Ablation (Section 6.3), in the last column of Table 5, we show that without the random partition strategy, CARL would collapse. We appreciate the feedback. We will rewrite this Ablation section to make it clearer about the limitations of CARL, shown in Table 5. 

Also, please note that the slow/fast encoders are optional. Table 5 also shows that CARP does not need a momentum encoder as BYOL does. However, adding such an encoder boosts the performance, as shown in Table 5. 

> The authors are highly encouraged to add some diagrams to help to explain the random partition in section 4. The consistency assignment with random partitions is hard to understand for readers.

**Response**:  We thanks the reviwer for the feedback. We will incorporate an image to better explain the consistent assignment of views over random partitions. 

> As the authors claimed, the number of partition blocks can greatly affect the results. Are there any methods to quickly select the best number? Or are there any solutions to automatically decide the number?

**Response**:  In the paper, Tables 5 and 7 explore different properties regarding how to deal with the creation of random partitions. In Table 5,  we performed a hyperparameter search to find the optimal number of partition blocks. In Table 7, we explore a different way of creating the partitions. Namely, we contrast creating the partition blocks at the beginning of training and keeping them fixed throughout training against recreating the partition blocks at every training iteration.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a representation learning method based on clustering.
Their idea is to cluster data using a lot of prototypes while ensuring that (1) different augmentations of the same input are assigned to the same cluster; (2) that all the clusters are used (to avoid a collapse)
Since the number of clusters might be (and also needs to be) larger than the batch size, the authors create a random partition of the prototypes at each iteration and apply the loss to each of these. 
The model performs better than the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ Simple idea, efficient that works.
+ paper easy to read

- no theory behind
- reported experiment scores are lacking rigor
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The text is easy to read and clear. They use the supplementary to describe the different experimental settings which is fair.

The main novel lies in the partitioning of the clusters. It novel for that problem but not for all. For example:
*Guha, S., Rastogi, R., & Shim, K. (1998). CURE: An efficient clustering algorithm for large databases. ACM Sigmod record, 27(2), 73-84.*
It can also be interpreted as a hierarchical clustering or an ensemble-based clustering method.
These random partitions could also be seen as random projections where the center of the centroids are remembered:
*Ye, M., Liu, W., Wei, J., & Hu, X. (2016). Fuzzy-means and cluster ensemble with random projection for big data clustering. Mathematical Problems in Engineering, 2016.*
*Lai, Y., He, S., Lin, Z., Yang, F., Zhou, Q., & Zhou, X. (2019). An Adaptive Robust Semi-Supervised Clustering Framework Using Weighted Consensus of Random $ k $ k-Means Ensemble. IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and data engineering, 33(5), 1877-1890.*

Fo representation learning there is this unpublished work:
*https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10419*


Regarding reproducibility: Yes it is. The model seems fairly simple to implement and a PyTorch code is provided.
Except for the results in the tables. It is not clear if these are averages or best run. The differences cannot be judged without a t-test (or similar). This is standard practice. It's not because others didn't do it, that we should allow this loop to keep going.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is easy to read. The idea is elegant. The results are good.

The experimental setup is for me the weakest point since we don't know if these are best runs or averages. For example, you claim to report the best Top1 in the first section of Table 1 with 71.7 while the challenger is 70.6. It's not far.
Better example: same table same section mAP score. CARP reaches 85.6 and is marked bold. while PCLv2 achieves 85.4 and is not highlighted. 
This is a standard mispractice.
Don't get me wrong. I'm not saying you hide anything. I am convinced of your model. I'm just saying we should stop reporting results like that.

I regret the lack of theory.
for example, instead of the entropy, have you tried a KL divergence? This would allow you to interpret that as a Dirichlet prior.
As for Lc, maybe you could explain why it reaches its minimum when s=t. I believe it has to do with the softmax.

TYPOS:
Page 2, contribution 2: "not require normalization tec[h]niques."

Section 3 paragraph 2:
You begin with $\Phi$ for the prototypes and then move to $C$. Maybe this should be harmonized.

Section 2 paragraph 3: "N_P = [K/N_P]"  I guess it should be [K/N_B].
Also, since you ask N_B to divide K, so the brackets are superfluous.

Later you use j as an index for the partitions, but you used j to index something else earlier.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Comments on novelty and the experimental setup
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time and comments. We will incorporate the feedback to make the paper better.

> The main novel lies in the partitioning of the clusters. It novel for that problem but not for all. For example: Guha, S., Rastogi, R., & Shim, K. (1998). CURE: An efficient clustering algorithm for large databases. ACM Sigmod record, 27(2), 73-84. It can also be interpreted as a hierarchical clustering or an ensemble-based clustering method. These random partitions could also be seen as random projections where the center of the centroids are remembered: Ye, M., Liu, W., Wei, J., & Hu, X. (2016). Fuzzy-means and cluster ensemble with random projection for big data clustering. Mathematical Problems in Engineering, 2016. Lai, Y., He, S., Lin, Z., Yang, F., Zhou, Q., & Zhou, X. (2019). An Adaptive Robust Semi-Supervised Clustering Framework Using Weighted Consensus of Random  k-Means Ensemble. IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and data engineering, 33(5), 1877-1890.

**Response:** We agree with the reviewer that the strategy of using partitions is not new, as it has been used on other algorithms and contexts before. Most importantly, as the reviewer agrees, the strategy of using partitions is novel in the context of self-supervised representation learning, and we show that it is effective for learning unsupervised visual representations. In this context, by bringing proven ideas and showing their benefit to new contexts, we benefit the community that will read the manuscript.

> The experimental setup is for me the weakest point since we don't know if these are best runs or averages. For example, you claim to report the best Top1 in the first section of Table 1 with 71.7 while the challenger is 70.6. It's not far. Better example: same table same section mAP score. CARP reaches 85.6 and is marked bold. while PCLv2 achieves 85.4 and is not highlighted. This is a standard mispractice. Don't get me wrong. I'm not saying you hide anything. I am convinced of your model. I'm just saying we should stop reporting results like that.

**Response:** We fully understand the concerns expressed by the reviewer regarding the experimental setup. All the results presented in the paper are single runs. Note, however, that these runs were not tuned or selected from a set of configurations (that is, we are not tuning the seeds of the runs).  Instead, they are the results after executing our proposal with a given set of hyperparameters. The reason behind that is the time it takes to run a single experiment and our limited resources. To give you an idea, each experiment in Table 1 takes more than a week with our hardware. For this reason, we can not afford to have multiple runs and report averages with standard deviations.
